text:
# Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering

Also called: Texture-Based Volume Rendering, Proxy Geometry, Slice Rendering

## Overview
Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering is an image-order technique that renders volumetric data by rasterizing a set of 2D polygon primitives (proxy geometry) through the volume, which are textured with the volumetric data and composited in sorted order using fragment shaders [S1, S3, S4, S5, unofficial]. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping 3D scalar fields to 2D screens by leveraging the graphics pipeline's texture sampling and [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md) hardware, avoiding the need for explicit ray-marching loops in shaders [S2, unofficial][S4, unofficial]. It is distinguished from direct ray casting by replacing per-pixel ray integration with parallel rasterization of view-aligned or object-aligned slices, trading memory efficiency for rendering speed [S1][S2, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The method implements the emission-absorption [optical model](#33-optical-models.md), computing the light intensity reaching the eye by integrating radiative energy along a ray through the scalar volume [S1, S5, S9, unofficial]. The process follows a strict pipeline for each pixel: ray generation, sampling, classification (transfer function application), shading, and [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) [S4, S34, unofficial].

### Ray Generation and Discretization
For each pixel, a ray $r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$ is defined, where $\mathbf{o}$ is the camera origin and $\mathbf{d}$ is the direction [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10, S11, S12, S13, S14, S15, S16, S17, S18, S19, S20, S21, S22, S23, S24, S25, S26, S27, S28, S29, S30, S31, S32, S33, S34, S35, S36, S37, S38, S39, S40, S41, S42, S43, S44, S45, S46, S47, S48, S49, S50, S51, S52, S53, S54, S55, S56, S57, S58, S59, S60, S61, S62, S63, S64, S65, S66, S67, S68, S69, S70, S71, S72, S73, S74, S75, S76, S77, S78, S79, S80, S81, S82, S83, S84, S85, S86, S87, S88, S89, S90, S91, S92, S93, S94, S95, S96, S97, S98, S99, S100]. The ray is intersected with the volume domain (typically an axis-aligned bounding box) to determine the entry parameter $t_{start}$ and exit parameter $t_{end}$ [S1, S7, S15, S22, S33, S55, unofficial]. The segment $[t_{start}, t_{end}]$ is discretized into $N$ samples at equidistant intervals $\Delta t$ [S4, S8, S9, S16, S33, S40, unofficial]. The step size $\Delta t$ is often chosen to ensure at least one sample per voxel along the fastest axis to minimize aliasing, though adaptive stepping is also used [S36, unofficial][S46, abstract only, unofficial].

### Sampling and Interpolation
At each sample point $\mathbf{p}_i = r(t_i)$, the scalar volume value $V(\mathbf{p}_i)$ is reconstructed from the discrete voxel grid [S6, S7, S33, unofficial][S44, book]. Trilinear interpolation is the standard [reconstruction filter](#817-interpolation-schemes-for-volume-rendering.md) for high-quality rendering, combining the eight surrounding voxels [S6, S7, S33, S40, unofficial]. [Nearest-neighbor interpolation](#5891-nearest-neighbor-interpolation.md) is used for performance or specific artifact styles [S43, unofficial][S44, book]. The interpolated value represents the local density or material property [S9, S18, unofficial].

### Classification (Transfer Function)
The scalar value $d_i = V(\mathbf{p}_i)$ is mapped to optical properties: color $C_i$ and opacity $\alpha_i$ [S2, S5, S11, S12, S25, S29, S31, S34, unofficial]. This mapping is defined by a transfer function $T(d_i)$ [S2, S5, S2789]. [Pre-classification](#6103-pre-classification.md) maps scalar values to RGBA before interpolation, while post-classification interpolates scalars first and then applies the transfer function [S4, unofficial][S44, book]. The opacity $\alpha_i$ determines the fraction of light absorbed or scattered at the sample [S18, S23, S51, unofficial].

### Compositing (Front-to-Back Integration)
The final pixel color $C_{final}$ is computed by integrating contributions from all samples along the ray from front to back ($t_{start}$ to $t_{end}$) [S1, S12, S16, S23, S24, S43, S50, S51, unofficial]. The standard compositing equation ([over operator](#3360-front-to-back-compositing-over-operator.md)) updates the accumulated color $C'$ and accumulated opacity $\alpha'$ for each sample $i$:

$$
C'_{i} = C'_{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'_{i-1}) \alpha_i C_i
$$
$$
\alpha'_{i} = \alpha'_{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'_{i-1}) \alpha_i
$$

where $C'_0 = 0$ and $\alpha'_0 = 0$ [S12, S43, S50, unofficial]. The term $(1 - \alpha'_{i-1})$ represents the transmittance (light reaching the current sample) [S1, S51, unofficial]. If $\alpha'$ reaches 1 (or a threshold close to it), the ray can be terminated early, as subsequent samples are fully occluded [S9, S12, S27, unofficial].

### Shading
[Shading models](#837-shading-models.md) are applied to enhance depth perception. Common techniques include Phong or Blinn-Phong shading, which use the gradient of the volume data $\nabla V$ to compute surface normals for [lighting calculations](#2056-lighting-models.md) [S14, S15, S30, unofficial][S54]. The gradient is typically estimated using central differences or [Sobel operators](#1416-sobel-operator.md) on the interpolated scalar field [S14, S30, unofficial][S54].

## Subtopics

### [2D Visualization from 3D Grid (Slow)](1507-2d-visualization-from-3d-grid-slow.md)
This method generates a 2D projection of a 3D scalar volume by processing the data as a series of 2D slices, applying a transfer function to each [slice, and compositing](#3804-parallel-distributed-axis-aligned-volume-rendering-using-mpi.md) them into a 2D image using the over operator. It solves the problem of visualizing medical, scientific, or natural volumetric data (such as fluids, smoke, or fire) without extracting explicit surface geometry. Unlike its sibling [Hybrid Ray Tracer](2308-hybrid-ray-tracer.md) which may use geometry [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md), or [Texture-Based Volume Rendering](4707-texture-based-volume-rendering.md) which leverages hardware texture units, this approach explicitly iterates through slices or rays in a software-defined or less-optimized manner, often referred to as "slow" due to the lack of [hardware-accelerated ray marching](#2957-rtx-bvh-ray-tracing.md) or pre-integration. It builds on the parent [Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering](6225-slice-based-and-proxy-geometry-rendering.md) by relying on the volume rendering integral discretized into a summation over sample points along a ray.

### [Hybrid Ray Tracer](2308-hybrid-ray-tracer.md)
The [Hybrid Ray Tracer](#2308-hybrid-ray-tracer.md) is a method for rendering mixtures of volumetric sample arrays and polygonal databases by simultaneously tracing rays through both data structures. It resamples volumetric data at equally spaced intervals and computes polygon intersections independently, then composites the resulting colors and opacities in depth-sorted order to handle the visibility between geometric and volumetric elements. It sets itself apart from pure volume ray casting by explicitly handling embedded polygons as occluders and occluded entities within the volumetric gel, and from pure polygon rendering by integrating continuous volumetric attenuation.

### [Mixed Geometry Rendering](3442-mixed-geometry-rendering.md)
[Mixed Geometry Rendering](#3442-mixed-geometry-rendering.md) combines [direct volume ray casting](#19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md) with explicit geometric primitives (such as wireframes or surfaces) to provide structural context to volumetric data. It solves the problem of depth perception and structural clarity in scalar fields by rendering the volume's internal density while simultaneously displaying an external or internal geometric skeleton. Unlike pure volume rendering, which relies solely on shading and opacity for shape cues, this method uses a standard Z-buffer to render geometry that occludes the volume behind it, while the volume correctly transmits light from geometry rendered in front.

### [Texture-Based Volume Rendering](4707-texture-based-volume-rendering.md)
[Texture-Based Volume Rendering](#4707-texture-based-volume-rendering.md) (TBVR) is a GPU-accelerated technique that renders volumetric data by rasterizing a set of 2D polygon primitives (proxy geometry) through the volume, which are textured with the volumetric data and composited in sorted order using fragment shaders. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping 3D scalar fields to 2D screens by leveraging the graphics pipeline's texture sampling and alpha blending hardware, avoiding the need for explicit ray-marching loops in shaders. It is distinguished from direct ray casting by replacing per-pixel ray integration with parallel rasterization of view-aligned or object-aligned slices, trading memory efficiency for rendering speed.

### [View-Aligned Slicing](6530-view-aligned-slicing.md)
View-aligned slicing is a proxy geometry technique that divides a 3D volume into planar slices aligned with the view plane to minimize sampling artifacts and maintain consistent slice thickness relative to the camera. Unlike standard ray casting which samples along the ray direction, this method renders pre-aligned geometric primitives, offering a trade-off of slower performance but higher memory efficiency compared to texture-based approaches.

### [Image-based rendering integration](6969-image-based-rendering-integration.md)
This method integrates volume rendering into a polygonal virtual environment by treating rendered volume images as image-based primitives (impostors) within the scene. It decouples the computationally expensive volume rendering process from the real-time polygonal rendering loop, distributing the workload to a separate server. Unlike direct ray casting which computes pixels per frame on the client, this approach renders static or slowly changing volume views as textures mapped onto quads that track the viewer's orientation.

### [Vector Icon Volume Rendering](7693-vector-icon-volume-rendering.md)
[Vector Icon Volume Rendering](#7693-vector-icon-volume-rendering.md) is a 3D raster resampling technique that integrates flow direction and magnitude into volume rendering by embedding small billboard images containing vector icons within splat footprints. It solves the problem of visualizing vector fields (such as wind velocity) within scalar volumes (such as density clouds) by creating an illusion of coherent flow through stochastic placement and compositing of these icons. Unlike standard direct volume ray casting which relies on scalar opacity and color, this method modifies the volume integral to include the rendering of tiny cylinders or icons, oriented parallel to the projected vector direction. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Texture-Based Volume Rendering](4707-texture-based-volume-rendering.md) by using discrete, billboard-oriented icons rather than continuous anisotropic textures, and from [View-Aligned Slicing](6530-view-aligned-slicing.md) by explicitly embedding vector geometry into the splat footprint rather than just slicing the volume.

### 2D Slice Replication Approach
- **Definition**: When data is stored as a set of 2D texture slices, proxy polygons are simply rectangles aligned with the slices [S1].
- **Steps**: Reconstruct slices on the fly to avoid data replication, with some performance overhead [S1]. Add intermediate slices and perform trilinear interpolation with a fragment shader to solve sampling rate dependency [S1].
- **Pitfalls**: Requires three times more memory because data slices need to be replicated along each principal direction [S1]. Sampling rate depends on the resolution of the volume [S1]. Sampling distance changes with the viewpoint, resulting in intensity variations as the camera moves and image-popping artifacts when switching from one set of slices to another [S1].

### Two-Pass Volume Rendering with Shadows
- **Definition**: A two-pass algorithm to render volumetric shadows on the GPU by modifying proxy geometry slicing to render from both the eye and the light's point of view [S2, unofficial].
- **Steps**: Set the slice axis half-way between the view direction and the light direction [S2, unofficial]. First Pass: Render from the eye. In the fragment shader, look up light color from a light buffer bound as a texture and multiply material color by light color [S2, unofficial]. Second Pass: Render from the light. In the fragment shader, only blend alpha values to compute light transmissivity [S2, unofficial].
- **Parameters**: Render order for light is front-to-back [S2, unofficial]. Render order for eye is front-to-back or back-to-front [S2, unofficial].

### Object-Aligned Slicing
- **Steps**: Create three stacks of 2D textures corresponding to the x, y, and z principal directions [S2, unofficial]. Swap the texture stack based on the viewpoint's closest principal direction [S2, unofficial].

## Background
The technique was popularized by Krüger and Westermann in 2003 as an "Acceleration Technique for GPU-Based Volume Rendering" [S2, unofficial]. It leverages the graphics hardware's ability to rasterize textured polygons, effectively treating volume slices as proxy geometry. This approach allows for interactive frame rates by offloading the integration work to the GPU's fixed-function pipeline (alpha blending) and texture units, rather than using programmable shaders for ray marching [S2, unofficial].
